tip: 'Die Brille' – feminine and singular for one pair in German, unlike English plural 'glasses'.
The whole phrase 'Trotz des schlechten Wetters' fills the first slot, so the verb comes next: 'gehen wir', not 'wir gehen'.
With no article the adjective carries the case ending: 'kalten Kaffee' shows the masculine accusative with '-en'.
'Der Lehrer' – masculine; '-er' is a common ending for male professions.
Bare time expressions normally take the accusative, which turns 'jeder' into 'jeden': 'jeden Morgen' means every morning.
With no article the adjective shows gender and case itself: 'frisches Brot' takes the '-es' that 'das' would otherwise carry.
Some masculine nouns add '-en' in every case except the nominative: 'der Komet' becomes 'einen Kometen'.
Sentence adverbs like 'leider' (unfortunately) or 'natürlich' (of course) can start a sentence; the verb then comes second, before the subject.
German has no -ing form; 'gerade' plus the present shows an action in progress: 'renovieren gerade', renovating right now.
'Fertig' alone already means both finished and worn out; 'fix und fertig' just intensifies it to completely wiped out.
'Den' is accusative because of its job inside its own clause: 'meine Mutter backt den Kuchen'.
'Heft' here means hilt or handle, not notebook: 'das Heft in der Hand' is holding the handle, that is, being in charge.
'Gestern' fills the first slot, so the verb 'ging' comes second – the subject 'ich' moves after the verb.
'Zwei linke Hände' is literally two left hands, the German version of being all thumbs.
'Ostsee' means 'Baltic Sea' – literally 'East Sea'.
'Biergarten' is literally 'beer garden' – a tradition from Bavaria of outdoor dining, often under chestnut trees.
'Helfen' takes a dative object, so in German you help to someone: 'er half seiner Nachbarin'.
For unreal conditions German uses special verb forms (Konjunktiv II): 'wäre' and 'könnten' instead of 'ist' and 'können'.
Without an article the adjective takes the ending itself: 'heißer Tee' carries the '-er' that 'der' would otherwise show.
Separable verbs split in commands: 'zuhören' becomes 'hör' and then 'zu', with the prefix stranded at the end.
'Ein Brett vor dem Kopf' is literally a board in front of your head, so you cannot see what is right there.
Future tense = 'werden' + infinitive at the end: 'werden ... umziehen'. The main verb stays in its dictionary form and closes the clause.
'Niemand' (nobody) adds '-en' as a direct object: 'niemanden'. The subject form stays plain 'niemand'.
Here 'schon' is a reassuring word meaning it will work out, not its other sense of already: 'wirst das schon schaffen'.
'Noch nicht' means not yet, literally still not: 'Ich bin noch nicht fertig'.
After 'nichts', an adjective is capitalized and takes '-es': 'nichts Falsches' = nothing wrong.
After 'ein' with a neuter noun, the adjective takes '-es' to show the gender 'ein' hides: 'ein rotes Kleid'.
'Eltern' (parents) exists only in the plural, so it always pairs with plural words: 'meine Eltern', never a singular form.
'Unterschreiben' keeps its prefix attached: 'unter-' is inseparable here, so it never splits into 'schreibt unter'.
'Bestehen' with a direct object means to pass a test: 'das Examen bestehen' = pass the exam.
